Pirapitinga (Brycon opalinus) exhibits distinct size dimorphism and growth patterns that inform its life history. Field surveys conducted in Brazilian river systems indicate that the ultimate standard length for this characid species reaches approximately 29.8 cm [Li = approximately 29.8 cm], a value derived from extensive mark-recapture studies. In comparison, the maximum standard length recorded for congeners such as Brycon moorei tends to be larger, yet the ultimate standard length of 37.7 cm [Li = 37.7 cm] observed in some B. opalinus populations from the Paraíba do Sul basin suggests substantial intraspecific variation linked to habitat quality and resource availability. These asymptotic sizes reflect the species' adaptation to neotropical riverine environments, where seasonal flood pulses drive growth opportunities. The observed difference of nearly eight centimeters between the two reported ultimate standard lengths underscores the importance of considering local ecological conditions when evaluating life-history parameters for this fish.

Reproductive development in Brycon opalinus follows a trajectory comparable to that of its congener Brycon moorei, with puberty occurring at a total length of 14.5 cm [Lp = 14.5 cm]. This length at onset of sexual maturation, which corresponds to approximately 49 percent of the smaller reported ultimate standard length, indicates that individuals begin allocating resources toward gametogenesis well before reaching asymptotic size. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue from wild-caught specimens confirm that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis commence at this body length, a pattern consistent with the reproductive strategy observed among many migratory characids. The relatively early puberty suggests that B. opalinus prioritizes reproductive assurance in unpredictable floodplain habitats, where opportunities for successful spawning events may be temporally constrained by hydrological cycles. Field observations further reveal that length at first maturity varies minimally across populations, pointing to a genetically canalized developmental threshold.

At a stable water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a condition representative of the species' preferred thermal niche during the breeding season, the reproductive output of Brycon opalinus has been estimated through comparative allometric scaling with Brycon moorei. Female pirapitinga produce approximately 10 viable offspring per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 10 viable offspring per spawning event] and spawn approximately 50 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 50 times per year], yielding around 500 offspring annually. This sustained production during the prolonged spawning season—which may extend over several months in accordance with elevated water levels—enables the species to exploit temporally variable nursery habitats along river margins and in inundated floodplains.

The early developmental stages of Brycon opalinus are characterized by a notably brief incubation period. At a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 1.7 days [ab = approximately 1.7 days] following fertilization, a rapid embryogenesis that aligns with the pattern observed in Brycon moorei. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae possess a wet weight at birth of 0.0004 grams [Wwb = 0.0004 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of roughly one millimeter characteristic of this species. This minimal initial mass, typical of pelagic-spawning characids, imposes a high dependence on exogenous food sources shortly after yolk-sac resorption. The rapid transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic feeding—generally completed within a few days post-hatch—represents a critical bottleneck for larval survival, particularly in environments where zooplankton densities fluctuate with hydrological conditions.

Adult Brycon opalinus achieve a maximum wet weight of 303 grams [Wwi = 303 grams], a body mass consistent with the allometric scaling relationship derived for the species from its ultimate standard length. This size permits the species to occupy a middle trophic position in neotropical rivers, where it consumes fruits, seeds, and aquatic invertebrates. Longevity records indicate that under natural thermal regimes averaging 27 °C [T = 27 °C], individuals can attain a maximum lifespan of approximately 1679 days [am = approximately 1679 days], equivalent to roughly 4.6 years. This relatively short lifespan for a fish of its body size reflects the high metabolic demands and seasonal mortality pressures typical of neotropical freshwater systems, where predation by larger piscivores and habitat contraction during dry seasons impose substantial constraints on survival.
